hero.headline: I build production web applications with Laravel and Vue.
hero.summary: From relational schema to deployed frontend. I've shipped corporate sites that real clients run themselves, an API serving both a web dashboard and a mobile app, and an open-source admin starter kit. Based in Kaohsiung, Taiwan — working with teams anywhere.

about.title: How I work
paragraphs: I'm a full stack developer finishing a Computer Science degree in Taiwan and continuing straight into a Master's programme. Most of my work happens in Laravel: designing the relational schema, writing the API layer, and building the admin tooling that non-technical staff actually use every day. My first production sites went live for paying clients during my internship, which taught me faster than any course that shipping is the halfway point — the code still has to make sense to whoever maintains it next.

I care about the unglamorous parts that decide whether a project survives its second year: clear boundaries between layers, permissions enforced in one place instead of scattered across controllers, and interfaces a content editor can use without being trained. When I don't understand something I read the source rather than guess, and I'd rather ship a smaller thing I fully understand than a larger one I don't.

projects.title: Selected work
projects.subtitle: Each of these started with a constraint rather than a feature list. Here is the problem, what I built, and what it changed.

sunyad.name: SunYad Corporate Website
sunyad.tagline: A corporate site for a real estate company, with a CMS its own staff operate.
sunyad.problem: The client wanted a premium corporate presence, but also needed to change banners, featured listings and section order themselves. A hand-coded site would have turned every content change into a developer ticket.
sunyad.solution: I built the public pages as reusable Blade components and backed each one with CMS-managed records. Administrators reorder sections, swap banners and update featured content from the admin panel, while the templates constrain what can change.
sunyad.outcome: The hardest call was how much freedom to hand the CMS. Full flexibility would have let staff break the layout; too little would have sent them back to us for every edit. I settled on structured per-component fields — the client owns the content, the design system owns the presentation.
features: Banner and featured-content management with drag-free ordering
Reusable Blade components shared across every page type
Responsive production frontend built to the client's brand
Admin panel usable by staff with no technical background

myson.name: Myson Corporate Website
myson.tagline: A rich-text publishing workflow that can't quietly wreck the layout.
myson.problem: Myson's team publishes content regularly, so the editing experience mattered more than feature count. Out-of-the-box WYSIWYG output drifts away from a site's typography and breaks layout consistency one paste at a time.
myson.solution: I customised the Summernote editor and the backend workflow around it: a constrained toolbar, sanitised output, and editor styles that mirror the public site so what an editor sees is what a visitor gets.
myson.outcome: Updates that used to require a developer now take minutes, and the site hasn't degraded into inconsistent typography — the usual price of giving non-technical users a rich-text field.
features: Customised Summernote editor with a deliberately limited toolbar
Sanitised rich-text output stored as structured content
WYSIWYG styles matched to the live site's typography
Backend CMS covering site-wide information and page content

stockAnalysis.name: Stock Analysis Platform & Mobile App
stockAnalysis.tagline: One Laravel API, a Vue dashboard and a Flutter app that never disagree.
stockAnalysis.role: Core full stack developer · Lead mobile engineer
stockAnalysis.problem: Comparing technical indicators across many stocks means switching between tools that don't agree on the underlying numbers. We wanted a single platform where the web dashboard and the mobile app read the same API and therefore the same data.
stockAnalysis.solution: I co-designed the MySQL schema and built the Laravel API on top of it, with Python pipelines parsing and normalising incoming market data. The web dashboard is Vue 3 with Chart.js for indicator visualisation; I owned the Flutter mobile client end to end, deliberately reusing the same API contract so the two clients cannot diverge.
stockAnalysis.outcome: The real design work was deciding what the API owns versus what each client computes. Putting indicator calculation server-side kept the Flutter and Vue clients thin and made both of them consistent by construction.
features: Laravel REST API serving a web and a mobile client from one contract
Python pipelines for parsing and normalising market data
Interactive Vue 3 + Chart.js dashboard for technical analysis
Cross-platform Flutter application built and shipped solo

laravelAdminStarter.name: Laravel Admin Starter
laravelAdminStarter.tagline: The week of setup work every Laravel project repeats, extracted into a starter that actually runs.
laravelAdminStarter.problem: Every Laravel project I shipped began the same way: authentication, a roles-and-permissions layer, CRUD screens, a content module, then containerisation. That is roughly a week before any product-specific code exists — and each rebuild quietly made slightly different authorisation decisions, which is precisely how security bugs get in.
laravelAdminStarter.solution: I extracted the groundwork into an opinionated starter, and made it a system rather than a set of management forms: the admin panel lives at /admin while the root is a public website reading the same catalogue, so an edit in the panel is visible to a visitor immediately. Sanctum in SPA cookie mode, RBAC as many-to-many tables with policies for per-record rules, a TipTap catalogue sanitised on write, a media library and an activity log — all on Docker Compose, so the host needs nothing but Docker Desktop.
laravelAdminStarter.outcome: 141 tests pass, and they target authorisation boundaries rather than happy paths: privilege escalation, self-deletion, drafts leaking past filters, passwords reaching the activity log, SVG reaching the media library. Two bugs still got through and were only caught by opening a browser after the suite was green — both are written up in the roadmap, because that lesson generalises.
features: RBAC with a Gate::before admin bypass, route middleware for features and policies for records
Bilingual UI across the SPA and the API, so validation errors arrive in the interface's language
TipTap product catalogue with per-language content, drafts and drag-and-drop public ordering
Media library with upload, preview and a picker wired into the editor's image button
Activity log that stays readable after the account or record it refers to has been deleted
Docker Compose stack: Nginx, PHP 8.4, MySQL 8.4, Redis 7 and Vite

openSource.title: Laravel Admin Starter
openSource.subtitle: An open-source Laravel 13 + Vue 3 admin panel and public website. Role-based access control, a bilingual interface, a WYSIWYG catalogue, a media library and an audit log — all running in Docker.
openSource.why: After the third project where I rebuilt authentication and a permission layer from scratch, it stopped being a coincidence and started being a missing tool. Worse, each rebuild made slightly different authorisation decisions — exactly the kind of inconsistency that becomes a security bug. I also wanted it to be a system that runs rather than a set of management forms, which is why the root of the application is a public website driven by the same catalogue the panel edits: a change made in the admin is visible to a visitor immediately.
challenges: Authorisation sprawl. The naive version scatters permission checks across controllers, views and route definitions, so nobody can answer "who may do this?" without reading the whole codebase. Roles and permissions became many-to-many tables, feature access moved into route middleware and per-record rules into policies — defined once, enforced everywhere.

Rich text that cannot become an XSS hole. Sanitising on output means a single forgetful template resurrects the vulnerability. I sanitise on write instead, so the database only ever holds safe HTML — which is what makes it defensible for the public site to render editor output at all.

One locale, two runtimes. Backend validation messages and frontend strings each want their own translation mechanism. Making them behave like one system, so an error arrives in the language the interface is actually showing, took more iterations than the permission layer did.

Testing boundaries instead of happy paths. The suite targets privilege escalation, self-deletion, drafts leaking past filters, passwords reaching the activity log and SVG reaching the media library. Two bugs still slipped through and were only caught by opening a browser after the tests were green.
architecture: HTML is sanitised on write, not on output. The database only ever holds safe HTML, so a template that forgets to escape cannot resurrect the hole.
Authorisation runs before validation, so an unauthorised caller gets a 403 rather than a 422 describing fields they should not know exist.
A draft returns 404, not 403 — a 403 would confirm the product exists.
Gate::before grants administrators everything except on their own account, otherwise rules like "nobody may delete themselves" never run for the account where they matter most.
Public API resources are allow-lists, so a column added later stays invisible to the website until somebody decides otherwise.
Polymorphic columns store short aliases rather than fully-qualified class names, so models can be renamed without breaking history that has already been written.
roadmap: SSR or prerendering for the public site — page meta currently only reaches crawlers that execute JavaScript
A raw-HTML editing mode behind a dedicated permission and a second, server-defined allow-list
Move mail and background jobs onto the Redis queue with a worker container
Screenshots and a written walkthrough for the decisions recorded in docs/ROADMAP.md
